name: Chloe Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Chloe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and we don't campaign for anything. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I pick for a health and beauty distribution centre that supplies a chain of chemist shops. I push a trolley with six plastic tubs round the aisles, shampoo, plasters, vitamins, nappies, and a handheld scanner tells me what goes in which tub. I do the early shift, seven till half three, and I'm one of the ones who checks the controlled stock cage.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being trusted with the cage, and I like the women on my aisle, we've been together five years. What wears me out is the walking, nearly twenty thousand steps a day. My partner Ryan drives lorries for a supermarket, and we bought a little terraced house two years ago, so the mortgage keeps me honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds sensible to me. I use a chatbot now and then to help write a birthday card poem, and that's about all it's good for. Our warehouse wouldn't notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but politely. At church people were worried last year about AI. I'd tell them it turned out to be a fancy spellcheck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved for me and Ryan. We've got seven months saved on top of the house, and both our jobs would just carry on. The mortgage is fixed for three more years, so we'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. I'd keep the early shift, keep the extra hundred a month going onto the mortgage, and start trying for a baby next year like we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Safe, really, like a Sunday afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned trying for a baby. How does work fit with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go part-time after, maybe three days, and Ryan would carry more of the bills. My mum lives two streets away and would help, which is how it should be. Family first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything worrying you even if AI changes nothing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ryan's hours, a bit. The supermarket keeps changing his routes and some weeks he's out until nine. But that's a normal worry, not an AI one.

say: AI turned out to be a **fancy spellcheck**, and I'd say so politely.
I'd reassure people at **church** who were worried last year.
think: I'm **relieved** because both our jobs simply carry on.
Seven months saved and a **fixed mortgage** keep us safe for now.
do: Keep paying an **extra hundred** a month onto the mortgage.
Start **trying for a baby** next year as planned, then go part-time.
feel: **Calm** and safe, like a Sunday afternoon.
S0.quote: At church people were worried last year about AI. I'd tell them it turned out to be a fancy spellcheck.
fieldNote: Her calm rests on **two incomes** and a fixed mortgage.
**Family plans** are already set and nothing here moves them.
Her only live worry is **Ryan's long hours**, not technology.

steps.text: Keep the early shift picking for the chemist chain
Pay an extra hundred a month off the mortgage
Start trying for a baby with Ryan next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office stuff goes first, the planning and booking. That's Ryan's route planners and the people who book his deliveries. My bit with the tubs stays for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the floor is fine and people shouldn't panic. I'd also say young people should look at apprenticeships rather than university, because the desk jobs are the ones going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry more for Ryan than for me. If AI plans my partner Ryan's lorry routes, the supermarket will squeeze more drops into every shift, and he's already out until nine. My job feels safe for a few years, but I've seen the tote robots at the new site on the bypass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my supervisor Gail if I can train as a stock controller, because that's the person who counts and checks the cage. I'd use the AI app more for our household budget, like my sister does. And we'd still try for the baby, maybe six months later than planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly for Ryan, and a little for the girls on my aisle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said stock controller. Isn't that more of a thinking job AI could take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm, maybe you're right. The counting is on a screen now. But someone still has to put their hands on the cage and sign for it, so I'd guess it lasts longer than booking lorries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ryan about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him not to wait for the company to look after him. He should get his crane licence or something extra on his card. He'd grumble, but he'd do it if I booked it.

say: The warehouse floor is fine for now, and nobody should **panic** yet.
Young people should choose **apprenticeships** over university, because desk jobs are going.
think: I worry more about **Ryan's routes** being squeezed than my own job.
I've seen the **tote robots** at the new site on the bypass.
do: Ask Gail about training as a **stock controller** for the cage.
Use the AI app more for the **household budget**.
Push the **baby plans** back about six months.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly for Ryan and a little for her aisle.
S1.quote: If AI plans my partner Ryan's lorry routes, the supermarket will squeeze more drops into every shift, and he's already out until nine.
fieldNote: Her worry centres on her **partner's job**, not her own.
She accepts a **gentle challenge** about stock control being screen work.
She'd **book Ryan's course** herself to make it happen.

steps.text: Ask her supervisor to train her as a stock controller
Use an AI budgeting app for household bills
Push trying for a baby back about six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's scary. Clever AI in 2028, then robots in 2031 that can do my aisle and drive my partner Ryan's lorry. That's both our wages gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after each other, families and churches, because the government won't move fast enough. I'd say companies that replace a whole town should help pay to retrain it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think we'd lose both incomes within a few years of each other. My job goes when the robots come, around 2031. Ryan's planning side goes first, and then the driving, and we've got a mortgage that comes off its fixed rate in 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Ryan and the bank and look at fixing the mortgage again for longer. I'd stop overpaying and keep every spare pound as cash. I'd put the baby off for now, which would break my heart, and look at a healthcare assistant apprenticeship at the hospital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing the maths on the mortgage, over and over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before the robots change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me time to get the healthcare apprenticeship done before my job goes. Looking after people in a ward is hands and heart, not just a screen. Three years is tight, but it's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said family and church should help each other. Would you take help from the government too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was training money, yes, gladly. A handout to sit at home, I'd rather not. But I'd be lying if I said I'd turn it down with a mortgage due. And my mum and the church would help with childcare once we did have a baby.

say: **Families and churches** need to look after each other, because government is too slow.
Companies that replace a town should **pay to retrain** it.
think: We'd likely lose **both incomes** within a few years of each other.
The **fixed mortgage** ends in 2029, right in the middle of it.
do: Meet the bank to **fix the mortgage** again for longer.
Stop overpaying and keep **spare money as cash**.
Apply for a **healthcare assistant** apprenticeship and put the baby off.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake doing the mortgage maths over and over.
S2.quote: Clever AI in 2028, then robots in 2031 that can do my aisle and drive my partner Ryan's lorry. That's both our wages gone.
fieldNote: The household faces a **double loss**: her picking and her partner's driving.
The **mortgage refix** in 2029 sharpens the fear.
She'd accept **training money** but squirms at the idea of handouts.

steps.text: Meet the bank to fix the mortgage for longer
Apply for a healthcare assistant apprenticeship at the hospital
Put trying for a baby on hold
Lean on her mum and church for childcare and support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, so 2031 for the AI and 2034 for robots. Like the fast one, it still hits both of us, just later. It feels more like weather coming than a flood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this one is a test of whether people take responsibility. You can see it coming, so plan. I'd tell the younger girls on my aisle to start a course now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd wait a year before doing anything big, until I saw other people do it first. Then I'd move. I don't like being the first one in the water, but I won't be the last either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd do the stock controller training, keep overpaying the mortgage, and try for the baby. Year two, if the news is real, I'd start the healthcare apprenticeship part-time. Ryan would do his crane licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have time, but both our jobs are on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the women on your aisle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Gail, my supervisor, that she should put on a lunch session about courses. Some of the girls have never filled in a form online. They'd need a hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We'd change jobs before we changed towns. Mum's two streets away and our church is here.

say: This one is a test of whether people **take responsibility**.
I'd tell the younger women on my aisle to **start a course** now.
think: I'd **wait a year** and watch others move first.
Both our jobs are **on the list**, just later than in the fast picture.
do: Finish **stock controller training** and keep overpaying the mortgage in year one.
Start the **healthcare apprenticeship** part-time in year two if the news is real.
Book Ryan onto a **crane licence** course.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to act but two jobs at risk.
S3.quote: We'd change jobs before we changed towns. Mum's two streets away and our church is here.
fieldNote: She **waits for proof**, then moves, and says so plainly.
Staying near **mum and church** is non-negotiable.
She'd help her **aisle colleagues** with online forms.

steps.text: Watch for a year before making big changes
Start a part-time healthcare assistant apprenticeship in year two
Try for a baby with Ryan as planned
Keep the early shift and the mortgage overpayments going

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” What's your first reaction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots by 2039. I'd be nearly 40 with a child at school. That gives us time to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a gift of time and people should use it. Learn a trade, save, keep your family close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine here. By the time robots can pick my tubs of shampoo and plasters, I'd have years in a hospital ward behind me. Driving is all my partner Ryan knows, and that worries me more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd have the baby as planned and go back part-time. Then I'd start the healthcare apprenticeship when the child is two. I'd push Ryan to do a plumbing course, because his brother is a plumber and could take him on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there in the background, but I'd feel like we have a plan and the time to carry it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ryan worries you more. What would you do if he wouldn't change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at him, kindly. And I'd make sure we kept enough saved to cover a year if he lost the driving. We'd manage on one wage for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI tools to plan any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably for the boring bits, like comparing courses or the budget. My sister swears by it now. I'd use it once she's shown me how.

say: Ten years is **a gift of time**, and people should use it.
Learn a trade, save, and keep your **family close**.
think: By 2039 I'd have years on a **hospital ward** behind me.
**Ryan's driving** worries me more, because it's all he knows.
do: Have the **baby as planned** and return part-time.
Start the **healthcare apprenticeship** when the child turns two.
Push Ryan toward a **plumbing course** with his brother.
feel: **Uneasy** in the background, but she has a plan and the time.
S4.quote: By the time robots can pick my tubs of shampoo and plasters, I'd have years in a hospital ward behind me.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her keep **family plans** and still retrain.
Her household risk now sits mostly with **her partner**.
She'd learn AI tools only after her **sister** shows her.

steps.text: Have the baby as planned and go back part-time
Start a healthcare assistant apprenticeship when the child is two
Keep a year of costs saved in case Ryan loses driving
Compare courses with an AI tool once her sister shows her

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes my job and Ryan's close together, right when our mortgage needs refixing. What would help is paid apprenticeships for people already working, and banks giving families like us a mortgage holiday while we retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who people would turn to. For me it's mum, the church and the women on my aisle. A robot can pick a tub, but nobody's going to bring soup to a robot when it's poorly.

headlineQuote: A robot can pick a tub, but nobody's going to bring soup to a robot when it's poorly.
portrait: Chloe is a 27-year-old picker at a **health and beauty** warehouse, trusted with the controlled stock cage.
She and her lorry-driver partner Ryan own a **terraced house** with a fixed mortgage.
She stays calm in the slow pictures but fears a **double job loss** in the fast one.
Her path out is a **healthcare assistant** apprenticeship at the hospital.
She waits to see others move first, and leans on **mum and church**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her job and Ryan's go close together around the **mortgage** refix.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for working people and a **mortgage holiday** while families retrain.
